# The architecture, plainly {#sec-architecture}

::: {.callout-warning title="Implementation audit correction"}
This chapter describes the intended architecture. The 2026-07-27 audit found
two material gaps between the contract and the public path: incoming effective
measure weights are stripped during `encode`, and the Barnes--Hut
approximation is not rotation equivariant because its spatial partition is
axis aligned. The exact dense backend retains the tested similarity contract.
See @sec-program-review before treating the opt-in measure or approximate
far-field statements below as established.
:::

This chapter is the **source of truth** for what the MeshTransformer *is*:
what goes in, what comes out, and what happens in between, in that order,
with as little jargon as we can manage. The mathematics behind each piece
lives in @sec-mesh-attention; the experimental evidence that shaped the
design lives in @sec-benchmarks and, blow by blow, in the lab notebook
(@sec-notebook). When the architecture changes because an experiment says it
should, **this chapter changes in the same commit.**

## What goes in, what comes out

The model computes one thing:

> Given the **boundary** of a domain — its shape, the *type* of boundary
> condition on each patch, and the boundary *values* — predict a physical
> field at **any set of points inside**.

Concretely, the input is a boundary mesh: a collection of small surface
elements ("cells" — line segments in 2D, triangles in 3D), each carrying

- its **position** (centroid), **size** (length or area), and outward
  **normal** direction;
- which kind of boundary condition it carries (Dirichlet, Neumann, …), as a
  one-hot label;
- the boundary **data** on it (a temperature, a flux, …), plus any global
  scalars (a material parameter) or global vectors (a far-field velocity).

The output is the predicted field at a list of **query points** — points,
not a grid, and each prediction is independent of which other queries were
requested. Nothing about the interior is given: no interior mesh, no
initial guess, no source terms (the problem class is homogeneous —
@sec-pde-theory).

## The forward pass at a glance {#sec-forward-pass}

The model is an encode/decode pair. **Encode** runs once per boundary;
**decode** runs for any number of query points afterward, reusing the
encoded boundary.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: >
%%|   The MeshTransformer forward pass, reference configuration. Encode runs
%%|   once per boundary in O(boundary cells); decode runs per query batch in
%%|   O(queries x boundary cells) and never lets query points interact.
flowchart TB
    classDef stage fill:#fff8e8,stroke:#8a6d1a,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef data fill:#eef4ff,stroke:#2a4a8a,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef out fill:#eaf7ea,stroke:#2a6a2a,color:#1a1a1a

    A["boundary mesh<br/>cells: centroid, size, normal,<br/>BC type, BC values"]:::data
    B["nondimensionalize<br/>(subtract boundary center, divide by<br/>intrinsic reference length =<br/>RMS boundary radius; explicit override)"]:::stage
    C["per-cell lift<br/>geometry &rarr; scalar + vector channels"]:::stage
    D["boundary self-attention &times; 1<br/>(every cell sees every cell,<br/>signed weights, no softmax)"]:::stage
    E["drive read-in<br/>(zero-preserving; linear, quadratic,<br/>homogeneous, or nonlinear mode,<br/>per problem)"]:::stage
    F["encoded boundary<br/>(cached; reusable)"]:::data
    G["query points"]:::data
    H["kernel decode, per query:<br/>exact single- + double-layer panel<br/>integrals &times; conditioned coefficients"]:::stage
    I["predicted field at queries"]:::out

    A --> B --> C --> D --> E --> F
    F --> H
    G --> H
    H --> I
```

In words:

1. **Nondimensionalize.** Subtract the boundary's (measure-weighted)
   center and divide by a reference length. The reference length is
   **derived intrinsically by default**: the measure-weighted RMS radius
   of the boundary about its center (the radius of gyration) — a smooth,
   differentiable function of the geometry itself. A user-supplied key
   remains available as an explicit override for applications with a
   canonical dimension (an aerodynamic chord, say). Why this matters:
   with the gauge computed from the geometry, scale equivariance is
   **unconditional** — there is no convention left for a caller to get
   wrong, because the last externally-trusted input has moved inside the
   architecture (evidence: @sec-intrinsic-gauge). After this step,
   nothing downstream ever sees an absolute position or an absolute
   scale.

   ::: {.callout-warning title="Using the override safely"}
   The guarantee above is a property of the **default path**. The
   override reintroduces exactly the failure mode the default
   removes, and the industrial campaign measured the cost: a
   hard-coded constant gauge made every DrivAerML-trained checkpoint
   diverge on zero-shot transfer to a different vehicle family
   (@sec-drivaerml-crossfamily). The rule this bought:

   > **If you must override, override with a similarity-covariant
   > functional of the input geometry — never a constant.**

   A declared chord or diameter that arrives *per sample*, scaling
   with the geometry, is fine and is what the knob is for. A number
   pinned in a config file is not a length; it is one dataset's
   absolute size wearing a length's units, and the model has no way
   to tell the difference.
   :::
2. **Lift.** Each cell's geometry and labels become a vector of latent
   *scalar channels* and a set of latent *vector channels* (next section
   explains the distinction and why we keep it).
3. **Boundary self-attention.** One attention layer lets every cell
   exchange information with every other cell — this is where the global
   character of an elliptic boundary-value problem lives. The couplings are
   *signed* (no softmax): boundary-integral kernels change sign, and a
   normalized, all-positive attention could not represent them.
4. **Drive read-in.** The boundary *values* (the "drive") enter through a
   layer that is **zero-preserving**: zero boundary data produces exactly
   zero output, for any weights — a homogeneous PDE with nothing driving it
   has the zero solution, and the architecture makes that structural. The
   read-in has four modes, chosen per problem. In *linear* mode the layer is
   additionally exactly linear in the drive, so superposition (doubling the
   data doubles the solution) holds to floating point — a guarantee worth
   taking **when** the governing PDE is linear, but a straitjacket when it
   is not. In *quadratic* mode the drive **degree is declared the way
   linearity is**: the linear machinery plus exactly one bilinear typed
   composition at the query read-in makes the output an exact
   degree-$\le 2$ polynomial in the drive for any weights — built for
   targets of known drive degree (a Bernoulli pressure is exactly
   quadratic), after the nonlinear mode's *implicit* degree ~21 was
   measured detonating off-range (@sec-nonlinear-fragility). In
   *homogeneous* mode the intended degree is one: the field state's
   O($D$)-invariant magnitude is factored out, a nonlinear typed map acts
   on the resulting direction, and the magnitude multiplies back.
   The implementation actually uses
   $F/(\lVert F\rVert+\varepsilon)$ with
   $\varepsilon=10^{-30}$, so degree one is approximate for positive
   scales comfortably above that floor, not an exact all-magnitude
   contract; it is also not odd after training. At ordinary tested
   magnitudes, a $k\times$ shift in drive statistics produces a
   $k\times$ shift in output rather than $k^{d}$; the learned map $g$
   sees a bounded near-unit state; and
   zero-preservation stays *exact even though $g$ carries biases*,
   because the magnitude multiplies back rather than being discarded.
   That last point is what a normalization layer cannot offer — discard
   the magnitude and $f(0)\neq0$ the moment anything downstream has a
   bias — and it is why this mode recovers bounded activations without
   surrendering the zero-drive contract. What it approximately gives up
   is amplitude nonlinearity
   ($u(\lambda g)\approx\lambda u(g)$ for $\lambda>0$ away from the
   floor), so it sits
   between *linear* (degree one **and** additive) and *nonlinear*
   (unbounded degree): the right declaration when the target depends
   nonlinearly on the drive's *shape* but roughly linearly on its
   *amplitude*, as nondimensional surface loads under a unit freestream
   do; the wrong one where amplitude nonlinearity is the physics, as on
   Liouville. Degree one is also the only one of these laws closed under
   composition, so it is the only one safe to stack
   (@sec-nonlinear-fragility). In
   *nonlinear* mode the drive enters through structurally
   multiplicative updates: zero-preservation survives, superposition is
   deliberately given up, and the model can represent nonlinear solution
   operators (this mode, not the linear one, broke the superposition wall
   on the Liouville benchmark). The program targets **any** steady PDE
   without interior data — linearity, like polynomial degree, is a
   property of a *problem*, offered as a contract, never an assumption of
   the architecture. One measured caveat: zero-preservation itself
   *presumes the homogeneous problem has the zero solution* — true for
   the linear class, an approximation for problems like Liouville, where
   zero boundary data has a nonzero interior solution and the contract
   pins the wrong value exactly (measured in
   @sec-stream-factorization).
5. **Kernel decode.** For each query point, the model evaluates the two
   classical singular kernels of potential theory — the single-layer and
   double-layer potentials — *exactly integrated* over every boundary cell
   (closed-form panel integrals, not point samples), and combines them with
   coefficients produced from the encoded boundary. The learning is in the
   coefficients; the singular structure is exact.

The reference configuration shown — one attention layer, two exact kernel
members, no other dictionary members — is the smallest configuration that
matches everything measured so far (~82k parameters; evidence in
@sec-benchmarks). Knobs exist to widen it (more layers, more members,
learned smooth members), and the notebook records what each knob was found
to be worth.

## Scalars, vectors, and the mirror test {#sec-typed-channels}

Every latent quantity in the network is one of exactly two types, and the
distinction is physical, not a software convenience.

An **invariant scalar** is a number that every observer agrees on no matter
how the scene is rotated or reflected: a temperature, a distance, a dot
product of two arrows. A **polar vector** is an ordinary arrow — a
displacement, a velocity, a surface normal: rotate the scene and the arrow
rotates with it.

There is a third kind of quantity we deliberately *exclude*, and the
cleanest way to see it is the **mirror test**. Hold a spinning wheel in
front of a mirror. Its velocity arrows reflect like ordinary arrows — a
velocity pointing at the mirror comes back pointing out of it. But its
*angular momentum* arrow does something strange: the mirror image spins the
opposite way, so the reflected arrow points where the rule "reflect like an
ordinary arrow" says it shouldn't. Quantities like that — cross products,
curls, rotation axes — are called **axial vectors** (or *pseudovectors*).
Similarly a **pseudoscalar** is a number that flips sign in the mirror (the
signed volume of three arrows, for example).

```{python}
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The mirror test. A polar vector (velocity, left) reflects like an
#|   ordinary arrow. An axial vector (the spin axis of the wheel, right)
#|   comes back flipped relative to naive reflection: the mirror image spins
#|   the other way. The MeshTransformer carries scalars and polar vectors
#|   only; axial quantities are rejected at the type level.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.4, 3.0))
for ax, title, flipped in ((axes[0], "polar vector (velocity)", False),
                           (axes[1], "axial vector (spin axis)", True)):
    ax.axvline(0, color="#0b0b0b", lw=2.5)
    ax.text(0, 1.32, "mirror", ha="center", fontsize=9, color="#0b0b0b")
    circle = plt.Circle((-1.0, 0.0), 0.52, fill=False, color="#52514e", lw=1.4)
    ax.add_patch(circle)
    circle2 = plt.Circle((1.0, 0.0), 0.52, fill=False, color="#52514e",
                         lw=1.4, ls="--")
    ax.add_patch(circle2)
    if not flipped:
        ax.annotate("", xy=(-0.35, 0.0), xytext=(-1.0, 0.0),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="#2a78d6", lw=2.4))
        ax.annotate("", xy=(0.35, 0.0), xytext=(1.0, 0.0),
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="#2a78d6", lw=2.4,
                                    ls="--"))
    else:
        for cx, up, ls in ((-1.0, True, "-"), (1.0, False, "--")):
            dy = 0.62 if up else -0.62
            ax.annotate("", xy=(cx, dy), xytext=(cx, 0.0),
                        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="#e34948",
                                        lw=2.4, ls=ls))
            theta = np.linspace(0.35 * np.pi, 1.15 * np.pi, 40)
            direction = 1.0 if up else -1.0
            ax.plot(cx + 0.40 * np.cos(direction * theta),
                    0.40 * np.sin(direction * theta),
                    color="#52514e", lw=1.1)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlim(-1.9, 1.9); ax.set_ylim(-1.05, 1.5)
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
```

Why the fuss? Because the physics of our problem class has a symmetry:
rotate or reflect a domain and its boundary data, and the solution rotates
or reflects with it, with no handedness anywhere (a Laplace problem cannot
tell left from right). The clean way to guarantee a network respects this
is to allow only quantities with definite, correct behavior under rotations
and reflections, and to combine them only in ways that preserve that
behavior. In representation-theory language, scalars and polar vectors are
two **irreducible representations** ("irreps") of the rotation-reflection
group — the smallest families of quantities that transform only among
themselves. We use exactly these two irreps and no others; anything a layer
tries to produce outside them is rejected at construction time rather than
silently mangled.

The combination rules are the ones your hands already know:

- scalar × scalar → scalar; any function of scalars is a scalar;
- dot products of vectors → scalar (this is how vector information reaches
  scalar channels);
- scalar × vector → vector; sums of vectors with scalar coefficients →
  vector (this is the *only* way the network makes new vectors — it never
  invents an arrow from nothing).

The practical consequence is strong: no layer ever sees a raw coordinate,
so equivariance holds **to machine precision, for any weights** — measured
at ~3×10⁻⁷ on trained models under rotations, reflections, translations,
and 0.2–5× rescalings (@sec-transolver compares this to the ~0.1 of a
coordinate-consuming baseline). Boundary *scalar* data rides along freely
through all of this — scalars are directionless, so they can modulate
everything without ever breaking the symmetry.

This refusal is not hypothetical: it has been measured, diagnosed, and
lifted. When a benchmark's target was a pseudoscalar, the model refused
it exactly as the type system predicts (relative error ~1.0, every
seed) rather than faking handedness from noise — and the principled
fix was one **opt-in extension for parity-odd 2D problems**: pseudoscalar
channels with the wedge product as a typed operation. (Irrep labels,
used from here on: `0e` = ordinary even scalar, `0o` = pseudoscalar,
`1o` = polar vector.) The 3D analogue (axial vectors) remains excluded,
and the reference configuration of @sec-reference-config is unchanged.
The full measured arc — wall, diagnosis, resolution, five-seed
confirmation — is @sec-fluid-suites.

## Attention as a boundary solve {#sec-attention-role}

Why attention at all? Elliptic boundary-value problems are global: the
solution at one end of the domain depends on boundary data at the other
end. Classical boundary-integral methods make this global coupling explicit
by solving a dense linear system over all boundary elements. The
MeshTransformer's boundary self-attention is the learned analogue: every
cell reads a weighted combination of every other cell's state, with weights
computed from geometry. Three departures from textbook transformer
attention, each forced by physics:

- **signed weights, no softmax** — integral-equation kernels take both
  signs;
- **quadrature weighting** — cells contribute in proportion to their
  surface measure, so refining the mesh converges instead of double-counting;
- **separable (low-rank) form** — the all-pairs coupling is factored
  through a small set of global "moments," making encode O(cells) instead
  of O(cells²) per layer. What that factorization *cannot* represent, and
  how the decoder compensates, is the subject of @sec-ceiling.

How much attention does the physics actually need? Measured answer: **one
layer, one full-width head**. On every all-Dirichlet benchmark, even
*zero* layers nearly suffices (the boundary system is dominated by its
local part — a second-kind Fredholm property; see @sec-encoder-depth); on
mixed Dirichlet/Neumann problems, where the boundary solve is genuinely
nonlocal, zero layers becomes unreliable and one layer restores full
accuracy (@sec-mixed-bc). Splitting that layer into multiple heads at
fixed total score capacity turned out to be pure bookkeeping — one
full-width head matches or beats it everywhere measured
(@sec-one-head-cross-suite).

## The decoder: classical kernels, learned coefficients {#sec-decoder-role}

The decoder answers: *given the encoded boundary, what is the field at
point $x$?* Its form is lifted directly from potential theory. Any solution
of a homogeneous elliptic problem can be written as boundary integrals of
known singular kernels against unknown boundary densities — that is the
Green representation (@sec-pde-theory). The decoder mirrors it:

$$
u(x) \;=\; \sum_{\text{cells } j}
\Big[\, c^{S}_j(\text{encoding})\cdot
\underbrace{\textstyle\int_{\text{cell }j} G\, \mathrm{d}s}_{\text{single layer}}
\;+\; c^{D}_j(\text{encoding})\cdot
\underbrace{\textstyle\int_{\text{cell }j} \partial_n G\, \mathrm{d}s}_{\text{double layer}}
\,\Big],
$$

with two crucial choices. First, the panel integrals are **closed forms**,
exact for every query-cell pair including queries arbitrarily close to the
boundary — "singular kernels need singular quadrature" is the program's
oldest lesson, and point-sampling these integrals is the classic way to
lose an order of magnitude near walls. Second, everything *learned* is in
the smooth coefficients $c_j$, produced per cell (and per head) from the
encoded boundary state. The division of labor is the chapter's motto:

> **The dictionary carries the singularity; the conditioning carries the
> smoothness.**

Earlier configurations also carried polynomial and free-form (MLP) "smooth
members" alongside the exact kernels. Systematic ablation removed them: on
linear problems they ranged from useless to actively harmful for
extrapolation, and the two exact members alone are best-in-class on every
linear benchmark (the nonlinear mode is the exception — there the
polynomial members are load-bearing; @sec-dictionary-ablation and
@sec-single-layer hold the evidence). The far-field study added a second
design rule to the motto: **learned coefficients should be bounded
functions of query position — trust nothing learned beyond its data —
with all radial physics carried by exact, licensed structure**; the
corresponding knobs (bounded gates, a compactified query source, an
$r^{-2}$ drive envelope, a monopole-free single layer) are **opt-in**,
licensed per problem class, and the reference configuration below is
unchanged (@sec-farfield-ladder).

One further opt-in contract extends the smooth members rather than the
exact ones: a **declared auxiliary length scale**
(`kernel_auxiliary_scale_key`). Some problems carry a second physical
scale the reference gauge cannot see — on AirFRANS the boundary layer
lives at $\delta/c \sim \mathrm{Re}^{-1/2} \approx 5\times10^{-4}$, and
the pilot's velocity error concentrated exactly there (49% of MSE inside
$d/c < 10^{-4}$) while every pair-radial feature was chord-scale. The
contract declares it: a rank-0 global operator field supplies the
dimensionless per-case ratio $\lambda = \delta/L_{\mathrm{ref}}$ (e.g.
$\mathrm{Re}^{-1/2}$), and the decoder appends a second copy of its pair
invariants rescaled to the $\delta$ gauge, feeding the learned smooth
members only — its carrier is the member MLP (so the knob requires MLP
members, which the reference configuration omits) and the exact members
are untouched. Because $r$ is already gauge-normalized and $\lambda$ is a
declared dimensionless input, similarity covariance holds by
construction. Licensed per problem class, exactly when such a scale is
physically known; default off.

One declared *mode* extends the decoder to boundary→boundary tasks: the
**boundary-trace mode** (`trace_of: <boundary>`). A layer potential is
discontinuous across its own layer — the classical **jump relation**: the
double layer's exterior and interior traces differ from the principal
value by $\pm\sigma/2$ — so a query sitting exactly ON a source panel
receives whichever branch of the discontinuity floating point happens to
land on (measured on DrivAerML: the *interior* branch $-1/2$, while
surface pressure and shear are the *exterior* trace $+1/2$; no learned
coefficient can repair a term that flips sign under infinitesimal
displacement — the GeoTransolver-gap verdict, @sec-nb-geot-gap-verdict).
The mode declares that the query mesh IS the named boundary's cell
centroids, index-aligned, and that declaration licenses exactly two
changes: the double layer's own-panel entries take the declared exterior
side's one-sided limit — exactly $+1/2$ in both 2D and 3D, the side the
cell normals point toward; the on-panel principal value vanishes for flat
panels, and the single layer needs no value correction because it is
continuous across the layer (only its normal derivative jumps) — and each
query gains typed read-outs of its *own* cell's post-attention encoded
state, the information flow the interior contract rightly denies bare
interior points but a declared trace query legitimately owns (Dirichlet
data IS the trace on Dirichlet patches). Equivariance is untouched (the
read-out is a typed projection of typed state), drive-linearity and zero
preservation survive (the drive read-out is bias-free and linear), and
query independence survives as independence *given the declared identity
map*. Licensed exactly when the queries are the source boundary's own
cell centroids on a declared side — surface loads on the body that drives
the flow; default off, bitwise.

Because each query's decode reads only the cached encoding and its own
position, predictions are **query-independent** — bitwise, by test: asking
for one point or a million, in any order, gives identical values at shared
points. Evaluation streams and parallelizes trivially.

The same independence sets the decode's cost and its one training-memory
knob. The dense evaluation is $O(N_qN_s)$ work, chunked over queries so
the *forward* peak is one chunk; during training, however, autograd
retains every chunk's pair activations, and that retained $O(N_qN_s)$ is
the measured product-scope wall (@sec-scale). The
`kernel_checkpoint_query_chunks` knob recomputes each chunk's activations
in the backward pass instead of retaining them — and because the decoder
is RNG-free and shape-deterministic, the recomputation is *bitwise*: the
knob changes what is stored, never the operator, its outputs, or any
gradient (asserted by test in all field modes, with the pseudo sector,
and in 3D). The price is one extra decode forward inside each backward.
Default off.

## What the architecture refuses to do

Each refusal is a falsifiable contract with a test attached, not a slogan:

| Refusal | Why | Where tested |
|---|---|---|
| Never read absolute coordinates or orientations | equivariance to machine precision for any weights | similarity-contract eval, every run |
| Never mix scalar/vector types outside the allowed products | no symmetry leaks, no hidden pseudo-quantities | construction-time rejection + unit tests |
| Never couple query points to each other | streaming evaluation; predictions independent of the query set | bitwise row-stability tests |
| Never respond to zero drive | homogeneous problems with no data have the zero solution | zero-drive eval, every field mode |
| Never break superposition *in linear mode* | when the problem is linear, its law should be structural, not learned | drive-linearity contract eval |
| Never point-sample a singular kernel | near-boundary accuracy | quadrature-vs-closed-form tests to ~1e-14 |
| Never depend on the *magnitude* of the quadrature measure (opt-in) | intended units invariance in the measure dimension | synthetic internal-rescale test only; upstream effective weights are currently stripped (@sec-program-review) |

The last row is newer than the others and is not yet a public-input
contract. `measure_normalization` is opt-in and bitwise-inert when off,
but `MeshTransformer.encode` reconstructs geometry-only meshes after
deleting incoming cell data. Thus composed Horvitz--Thompson weights do
not reach the normalization or decoder; only reconstructed geometric
areas do. Existing measure-rescale tests establish an internal algebraic
property, not correctness of the production intervention. Repair the
data path and add an end-to-end nonuniform-weight test before deciding
whether the default should flip.

## Reference configuration {#sec-reference-config}

The configuration that current evidence selects (the "emerging
architecture" of @sec-future), used as the default comparison arm:

| Piece | Setting | Parameters |
|---|---|---|
| Typed lift | scalar + vector channels (32/8 operator, 48/12 drive) | — |
| Boundary self-attention | **1 layer**, **1 full-width head**, separable rank 48 (scalar) + 16 (vector) | — |
| Drive read-in | zero-preserving; linear mode on linear benchmarks, quadratic or homogeneous (declared-degree) mode on known-degree targets, nonlinear mode otherwise | — |
| Decoder dictionary | **2 exact members** (single + double layer), 0 smooth members | — |
| Total | | **81,547** |

Caveats that keep this a synthesis rather than a verdict: the vector
channels are prunable on easy 2D geometry but load-bearing in 3D and on
parametric problems (keep them); the single-layer member costs some
extrapolation on very easy geometry while being decisively necessary on
hard geometry; the nonlinear field mode re-admits polynomial members;
and the one-head setting (flipped from 4 heads at matched total score
capacity $H(R_0+DR_1)$ — heads $H$, scalar/vector separable ranks
$R_0$/$R_1$, defined in @sec-mesh-attention — by the cross-suite rule,
@sec-one-head-cross-suite) rests on a decisive 2D-Laplace win plus
three-suite *non-inferiority* — it reverts if any suite ever shows a
decisive one-head loss. The frozen benchmark capacity configuration
(4 heads, ranks 12/4, two encoder layers) is unchanged for
comparability with every archived arm.
Chapter @sec-benchmarks carries every number; the notebook (@sec-notebook)
carries every step of how they were obtained.
